title: Functions
description: Package code into reusable building blocks with parameters, return values and scope.

subLevels.title: Defining functions
subLevels.summary: Write your own reusable commands with def.

blocks.text: You already use functions: print(), input(), int() and range(). A function is a named block of code that does one job. Now you will write your own.

items: Write the code once, use it many times
Give a clear name to a piece of work
Keep long programs tidy and easier to fix

blocks.text: A function is a reusable, named set of instructions.

blocks.code:
def greet():
    print("Hello!")
    print("Welcome to PyPath")

greet()
greet()
blocks.output:
Hello!
Welcome to PyPath
Hello!
Welcome to PyPath
explanation: def starts a function definition. greet is its name.
The empty ( ) and the colon : are required.
The indented lines are the function's body.
greet() calls the function — each call runs the body once.

blocks.text: Python reads your file from top to bottom. Defining a function does not run it — it only remembers it. The body runs when you call it.

explanation: The call on line 1 happens before Python has read the def.
Python stops with a NameError.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Calling a function above its def. Always put the def first and the call below it.

questions.prompt: Which keyword starts a function definition?
questions.explanation: Python uses def. Other languages use words like function, which is why it's a common guess.
The def is only remembered, not run. print("B") runs first, then show() prints A.

options: Function names must be written in capitals
The colon : is missing at the end of the def line
questions.explanation: Like if and for, a def line ends with a colon. Lowercase names and an indented body are correct.

options: Nothing, the function is never called
questions.explanation: beep() is called three times and each call prints beep once.
questions.code:
def beep():
    print("beep")

beep()
beep()
beep()

questions.prompt: What happens when Python reads a def block?
options: It remembers the function but does not run its body yet
It deletes the function after one call
questions.explanation: The body only runs when the function is called. That's why you can define a function and use it many times later.

subLevels.title: Parameters
subLevels.summary: Pass values into a function so it can work with them.

blocks.text: A parameter is a variable in the brackets of the def line. When you call the function, the value you pass is stored in it.

explanation: name is the parameter.
In the first call name is "Asha", in the second it's "Ravi".

blocks.text: Separate parameters with commas. Values are matched in order.

blocks.code:
def add(a, b):
    print(a + b)

add(2, 3)
add(10, 5)
explanation: In add(2, 3), a is 2 and b is 3.
In add(10, 5), a is 10 and b is 5.

items: Parameter: the name in the def line, like pet
Argument: the actual value you pass in the call, like "Tom"
Arguments are matched to parameters by position

blocks.code:
def describe(pet, age):
    print(f"{pet} is {age} years old")

describe("Tom", 3)
describe(3, "Tom")
blocks.output:
Tom is 3 years old
3 is Tom years old
explanation: Swapping the arguments swaps the values.
Python doesn't know what you meant — order matters.

blocks.output: TypeError: square() missing 1 required positional argument: 'n'
explanation: square needs one value for n.
Calling it with empty brackets is an error.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Calling a function with fewer (or more) arguments than it has parameters.
Each parameter needs a value when the function is called.

questions.explanation: word holds "Hi", and + joins it with "!". The name word is not printed — its value is.

questions.prompt: In def area(width, height):, what are width and height?
questions.explanation: The names in the def line are parameters. Arguments are the values you pass when calling, like area(3, 4).
a is 3 and b is 10 because arguments are matched in order, so a - b is -7.

subLevels.title: Return values
subLevels.summary: Send a result back from a function with return.

blocks.text: return hands a value back to the code that called the function. You can store it in a variable.

blocks.code:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

result = double(4)
print(result)
explanation: double(4) works out 4 * 2.
return sends 8 back.
result stores the returned value.
square(3) returns 9 and square(4) returns 16.
You can use them in maths just like numbers: 9 + 16 = 25.

blocks.text: print shows a value on the screen. return gives it back to your code. They are not the same.

blocks.code:
def shown(n):
    print(n * 2)

def given(n):
    return n * 2

a = shown(5)
b = given(5)
print(a)
print(b)
explanation: shown(5) prints 10 but returns nothing.
A function without return gives back None, Python's "no value".
given(5) returns 10, so b holds 10.

blocks.text: If you need to use the result later, return it.

explanation: For 20, the first return runs and the function ends immediately.
For 12, the if is skipped and the second return runs.
a + b is worked out, then thrown away.
Nothing is returned, so the call gives None.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Writing the calculation but forgetting the word return. The function then gives back None.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Lines after a return inside the same block never run.

questions.explanation: x * 3 with x = 4 is 12, and return sends it back to print. 7 would be 4 + 3, which is not what * does.
f prints 3 but has no return, so y is None. Both lines appear: first 3 from inside f, then None.
questions.code:
def f(x):
    print(x)

y = f(3)
print(y)

options: Prints the value on the screen
Sends a value back to the caller and ends the function
Repeats the function from the top
Saves the value to a file
questions.explanation: return gives a value back to the code that called the function. Showing it on screen is print's job.

questions.prompt: This prints None instead of 10. What's the problem?
options: w and h must be named width and height
result must be printed inside the function
questions.explanation: result is calculated but not returned, so the call gives None. Adding return result fixes it.
-2 < 0 is True, so the first return runs and the function ends. The second return is never reached.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so print(add(1, 2)) shows 3.
questions.explanation: return a + b sends 3 back to print. Using print inside would show 3 but then print(add(1, 2)) would also show None.

subLevels.title: Default and keyword arguments
subLevels.summary: Give parameters default values and pass arguments by name.

blocks.text: A parameter can have a default value. If the caller leaves it out, the default is used.

blocks.code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    print(f"{greeting}, {name}!")

greet("Asha")
greet("Ravi", "Welcome")
explanation: greeting="Hello" sets a default.
The first call doesn't pass a greeting, so "Hello" is used.
The second call passes "Welcome", which replaces the default.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Parameters with defaults must come after the ones without. def greet(greeting="Hello", name): is a SyntaxError.
You can pass an argument by naming its parameter: name=value. Then the order doesn't matter, and you can skip defaults you don't want to change.

blocks.code:
def order(item, size="medium", sugar=1):
    print(f"{size} {item}, sugar: {sugar}")

order("tea")
order("coffee", sugar=0)
order(size="large", item="juice")
blocks.output:
medium tea, sugar: 1
medium coffee, sugar: 0
large juice, sugar: 1
explanation: order("tea") uses both defaults.
sugar=0 changes only sugar; size keeps its default.
With keywords, item and size can be given in any order.

blocks.text: Defaults make arguments optional. Keywords make calls easier to read.

questions.explanation: times wasn't passed, so its default 2 is used and "ha" * 2 is "haha". No error, because the parameter has a default.
Keyword arguments are matched by name, not position, so name is "Mia" and age is 9.

questions.prompt: Which function definition causes a SyntaxError?
questions.explanation: A parameter without a default can't come after one with a default. The other three are all valid.

questions.prompt: When is a default value used?
options: When the caller doesn't pass a value for that parameter
Always, even if a value is passed
Only when the function returns None
questions.explanation: A passed value always replaces the default. The default only fills in when nothing is given.

subLevels.title: Scope
subLevels.summary: Learn where variables live: inside or outside a function.

blocks.text: A variable created inside a function is local: it only exists while the function runs. Outside the function, it's gone.

blocks.code:
def make_tea():
    cups = 2
    print(f"Making {cups} cups")

make_tea()
print(cups)
blocks.output:
Making 2 cups
NameError: name 'cups' is not defined
explanation: cups is created inside make_tea.
When the function ends, cups disappears.
The last line can't find it, so Python raises a NameError.

blocks.text: A variable created outside all functions is global. Functions can read it.

blocks.code:
shop = "PyCafe"

def welcome():
    print(f"Welcome to {shop}")

welcome()
explanation: shop is defined at the top level.
welcome() can read it without any extra work.

blocks.text: If you assign to a name inside a function, Python makes a new local variable — even if a global has the same name. The global is not changed.

blocks.code:
x = 10

def change():
    x = 99
    print(f"inside: {x}")

change()
print(f"outside: {x}")
explanation: x = 99 creates a local x inside change().
The global x is still 10.

blocks.text: Assigning inside a function creates a local variable.
The clean way for a function to change a value: take it as a parameter and return the new value. The caller decides where to store it.

blocks.code:
score = 10

def add_bonus(points):
    return points + 5

score = add_bonus(score)
print(score)
explanation: score is passed in as points.
The function returns 15.
The caller stores it back in score.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Expecting total = total + n inside a function to change a global total. Python treats total as local and raises an error. Pass it in and return it instead.

items: Local: made inside a function, lives only during the call
Each call gets fresh local variables

options: A NameError, because y only exists inside f
questions.explanation: y is local to f and disappears when f ends. Calling f() first doesn't make y available outside.
Functions can read global variables, so show() prints the global n.
a = 7 inside set_a creates a new local a. The global a is untouched and is still 3.
questions.code:
a = 3

def set_a():
    a = 7

set_a()
print(a)

options: A variable every function can change
A variable created at the top of the file
A variable created inside a function that only exists while it runs
questions.explanation: Local means "belongs to this function call". A variable at the top of the file is global.

options: Each call of a function gets fresh local variables
Local variables keep their values between calls
A function can't read variables from outside
questions.explanation: Locals are created again on every call and thrown away at the end. Functions can read globals, and parameters are local.

questions.prompt: Calling add(5) raises an error. What's the cleanest fix?
options: Pass total in and return the new value: total = add(total, 5)
questions.explanation: Assigning total inside the function makes it local, so total + n has nothing to read. Passing it in and returning it avoids the problem.
questions.code:
total = 0

def add(n):
    total = total + n

add(5)

questions.explanation: c is a fresh local variable on every call: it starts at 0 and becomes 1. The first call's c doesn't carry over, so it's not 2.
questions.code:
def count():
    c = 0
    c += 1
    return c

count()
print(count())
